content.content: The purpose of this page is to take you from having no idea how this synth works to writing your own presets as quickly as possible. Below the section "Writing a song" you'll also find a bunch of yapping about why the synth works the way it does, in case you're curious.

Bugsounds generates sound by playing lots of clicks very quickly so that they form a constant tone or note.

the speed and pattern at which clicks are played is controlled by the frequency editor using a notation language called clickCode. See the frequency editor help page for a description of the notation language.

Each click is made of a sequence of very short subclicks. You can control all aspects of a subclick through the Subclick Sequencer. 

To summarize the flow of click generation:
clickCode song -> click -> subclick -> generated audio.

Step 1: set up a simple subclick sequence with around 3 clicks. I reccomend setting the pitches first, then setting the levels, and then setting the lengths. Make sure it sounds right by clicking the preview button in the subclick sequencer header.

Step 2: Write the song in the frequency editor. (See the frequency editor help page for a guide on clickCode notation). Once the song is written, you MUST click the "Compile" button at the bottom of the page to send the new song to the synth. Here's a quick rundown of notation:

the base clickCode element is the note, which consists of a pair of values describing the end frequency and the note length respectively. 

For example this song: 440 1000, 220 1000, 0 1000 produces this series of pitches, rising from one pitch to the next in 1000 ms each time: 

[0]-1000ms-[440]-1000ms-[220]-1000ms-[0]

Note the beginning pitch is 0Hz. You can override this with a 1-length note at the beginning: 440 1.

The other elements are loops: [x, y, z] length, randomized values: rand(min max), variables: let x = value, and patterns: pattern(2 0 1). Patterns define the rhythm of click generation. They are very important for changing the timbre of the generated song.

Finally, if you want to refer to the frequency of the midi note you started the song with, the editors take a predefined variable midiFreq which represents this.

Step 3: Now that you have a song you're happy with, go back to the subclick sequencer and add or modify the subclicks. Also tweak the click settings to humanize it a little. Time rand is very good for that. See the click settings help page for an explanation of each parameter. 

Step 4: Optionally, if you want your song to use a resonator, turn it on by clicking the power button, and then write another clickCode song in the resonator editor to describe it's behavior. 

A couple important notes about the resonator editor: 

The resonator editor is compiled after the frequency editor, and it inherits all variables you used in the frequency editor. This can be useful for synchronizing them.

If the resonator editor's song ends first, it will loop back to the start and play again. 

Step 5: Use your finished song as is, or activate chorus mode to play it through a whole swarm of insects. Note that chorus mode can eat your whole CPU if you have a bunch of bugs playing at once with all the resonators on. Sorry!

Bugsounds is a synth designed to simulate insect stridulation/tymbalation for use in sound design and digital music. It uses a novel synthesis method similar to pulsar synthesis. When I set out to make a bug-based synthesizer, my first goal was to design something that accurately modeled the way that real insects generate sound. 

To start, the subclick sequencer models the specialized bodyparts that singing insects posess. Most singing bugs have a ridge of pegs, like the teeth of a comb, that they scrape a limb over. This produces a series of pitches. However, the sound each peg makes is so short and close together that they form a single note when we hear them. Cicadas have a different organs called tymbals, but they actually function in a similar way.

The next part I modeled was the notation language. It started as a way to combine an envelope with an LFO (a sequence of notes is equivalent to an envelope, and that same sequence placed in a loop becomes an LFO). all notes slide between values, since bugs very rarely change the speed of click generation instantly.

Another feature of clickcode notation is pattern blocks. This was born of a mistake I made in my prototype, causing clicks to be skipped. I noticed it sounded much more realistic, so I added it to my project! This, along with the randomization function, make clickcode adept at simulating bug song.

Chorus mode was one of the last bits of DSP I did. It takes the compiled song and subclick sequence, and bounces it around to a bunch of different voices, arrayed around the listener. It spatializes each voice applying reverb/lowpass/gain, and panning based on its' position relative to the listener. The other interesting part of chorus mode is the correlation algorithm.

Real insects have three strategies for deciding when to start singing. First, some insects wait for others of their species to stop before they start (alternation). Second, some species just get tired and wait a little bit, unconcerned about the singing of their neighbors. And third, some insects will try to sing over their neighbors to outcompete them (synchronization). One parameter, correlation, captures all three strategies, interpolating between them. -1 is alternation, 0 is random, and 1 is synchronization. 

I hope someone's found all this yapping interesting. If you have, and you have any questions, or you just make something cool, you can message me on discord (I'm "footbaal" on there).
